title: Zach Schroeder
text:
Email  GitHub  LinkedIn  Scholar  Résumé


I’m a behavioral scientist and statistician with seven years of experience researching interpersonal perception: how do we understand one another in person, online, and in the classroom? In doing so, my work has built analytic pipelines that transcribed and analyzed 20 years of video-recorded conversations to understand what the best cues are for understanding what someone is thinking, examined emotional and semantic drift in approximately 8 million Tweets discussing ‘cancel culture’ on social media, and used survey data to understand how students’ feelings of belonging impact how they interpret ambiguous academic feedback
Based in Minneapolis, if I’m not wrangling data at my desk, I’m either getting lost in the woods with my dog, trying to bake as well as my grandfather, or working on the NYT crossword.

title: Does the same personality carry the same consequences? Personality, race, sex, and school suspension
text:
In brief. Out-of-school suspension is handed out unevenly by race, and the usual explanation is behavior. I tested a different one: that the same personality trait is read differently depending on who has it. Using 6,351 students from two national longitudinal datasets, with a preregistered analysis plan, I modeled suspension, high school graduation, and college expectations as a function of personality, race, and sex. Trait anger predicted suspension far more strongly for Black boys (OR = 1.93) than for White girls, while self-reported delinquency showed no racial gap. The disparity tracks adult judgment more closely than student behavior.

N = 6,351NLSY79-CYAAdd Healthpreregistered (OSF)three-way interactionssimple slopes

title: Does the same personality carry the same consequences? Personality, race, sex, and school suspension
text:
Why this mattered
School discipline disparities are among the most litigated and most studied gaps in American education, and the debate usually stalls on one question: is the gap driven by what students do or by how adults respond? Personality gives a way in. If a trait like anger or low conscientiousness predicts suspension equally for everyone, the behavioral account holds; if the same trait predicts suspension only for some groups, the judgment account gains ground.

title: Does the same personality carry the same consequences? Personality, race, sex, and school suspension
text:
Data






NoteAccess



Both datasets are public but registration-gated. Study 1 used the Children and Young Adults of the National Longitudinal Survey of Youth 1979 (N = 1,255); Study 2 used Add Health Waves I and III (N = 5,096), for a combined analytic sample of 6,351 drawn from roughly 17,000 available records. Personality was measured with the 20-item Mini-IPIP and, in Add Health, NEO-PI-R anger and HPI anxiety and optimism items. Analysis code is public; person-level data are not redistributed.

title: Does the same personality carry the same consequences? Personality, race, sex, and school suspension
text:
What I did
The analysis was preregistered at osf.io/79wna. Continuous outcomes (PIAT math percentile) were modeled with OLS and binary outcomes (suspension, graduation, college desire and expectation) with logistic regression, each including the race × sex × trait three-way interaction and simple-slope contrasts for every trait so that the effect of a trait could be read separately within each group.

title: Does the same personality carry the same consequences? Personality, race, sex, and school suspension
text:
What I found
Black male students at high trait anger faced sharply elevated suspension risk (OR = 1.93); White female students at the same trait level did not. Self-reported delinquency, the behavioral control, showed no racial gap. The pattern is consistent with suspension disparities reflecting how adults interpret the same disposition in different students.

title: Does the same personality carry the same consequences? Personality, race, sex, and school suspension
section: What a team would do with this
text:
What a team would do with this
For a district or an education-technology company, the operational implication is that discipline and referral data cannot be treated as a clean measure of behavior; they measure behavior filtered through adult judgment. Any model that uses referrals as an outcome or a feature inherits that filter, and the fix is to model the interaction explicitly rather than adjust for race as a main effect and move on.

title: Does the same personality carry the same consequences? Personality, race, sex, and school suspension
text:
Limits
Personality is self-reported and measured once. The two datasets differ in instruments and cohort, so the replication is conceptual, not exact. Interaction effects in logistic models are sensitive to cell sizes, which is why the preregistration fixed the contrasts in advance.

title: Can a language model tell what a speaker is thinking? Validating automated measures of conversation against human coding
text:
In brief. People are confident about what others are thinking, and the words those others say often point somewhere else. My dissertation asked which features of speech predict how accurately a listener infers a speaker’s thoughts, using six studies collected over 20 years by different research teams (74 hours of conversation). Getting there was mostly measurement: automated transcription corrected by a trained coding team, a segmentation model fine-tuned on 5,000 hand-coded utterances (96.8% holdout agreement), a four-transformer ensemble for dialogue acts (93.4% on a 1,000-utterance human-coded holdout), sentence-embedding similarity between speech and inference, and two-stage Bayesian Gaussian process meta-analysis with prior and kernel sensitivity checks.

title: Can a language model tell what a speaker is thinking? Validating automated measures of conversation against human coding
text:
Why this mattered
Every team that runs a “listening” program, a sentiment tool, or a conversational model is betting that an automated reading of language tracks what people actually mean. This project is a controlled test of that bet: a setting where the speaker’s real thoughts were recorded at the time, so the automated measure can be scored against ground truth.

title: Can a language model tell what a speaker is thinking? Validating automated measures of conversation against human coding
text:
What I did
Consolidation. Six legacy studies, none designed to be combined, were transcribed with a speech model, corrected by research assistants I trained, and segmented into dialogue acts with a model fine-tuned on 5,000 hand-coded units. Definitions were written down as the dataset was built so that it could be reused without me.
Automated measures, validated. A weighted-majority ensemble of four transformer classifiers tagged each utterance’s dialogue act (question, suggestion, inform, acknowledgment, and so on), reaching 93.4% accuracy on a 1,000-utterance human-coded holdout, above published single-model benchmarks of 86 to 92%. Semantic similarity between what a speaker said and what a listener inferred was measured with sentence embeddings, with sensitivity checks across alternative embedding models.
Modeling. Each study was fit with a Bayesian multilevel Gaussian process model of similarity over conversation time (R, Stan), then pooled in a two-stage individual-participant-data meta-analysis. Prior specifications S0 through S6 and alternative covariance kernels were run for every model and compared by posterior overlap; model comparison used leave-one-out cross-validation.

title: Can a language model tell what a speaker is thinking? Validating automated measures of conversation against human coding
text:
What I found
The strongest signal of what a speaker was thinking sat in the plain content of their suggestions, and listeners mostly did not weight it. That gap, between an available cue and its use, is a tractable target for improving interpersonal accuracy, and it is exactly the kind of gap an automated measure can surface at scale.

title: Can a language model tell what a speaker is thinking? Validating automated measures of conversation against human coding
section: What a team would do with this
text:
What a team would do with this
Before trusting an automated reading of conversation, score it against human coding on a holdout, report the agreement, and run the analysis under alternative model choices to see what moves. The numbers on this page (96.8%, 93.4%, and the sensitivity comparisons) are the form that evidence should take.

title: Who cancels, and how angrily? Measuring the moral content of 8.6 million tweets
text:
In brief. Everyone has an opinion about cancel culture and almost nobody has data. I collected 8.6 million tweets across five kinds of cancellation (the meme itself, the “is over party” hashtag, canceled academics, celebrities, and private citizens), inferred each author’s partisan lean from their bio, scored every tweet for moral content with a dictionary and two transformer models, and asked what the moral temperature of cancellation actually looks like. Punishment framing dominates in every sample. Conservative-leaning users run slightly hotter on outrage, but the effect is small and I report it that way. The most reliable partisan difference is rhetorical, not volumetric: the right bundles “cancel culture” with woke, CRT, and SJW about 39% more often than the left.

8.6M tweets4.0M usersTF-IDF and semantic networksMoral FoundationsRoBERTa classifiersBERTopiccluster-robust effect sizesSLURM

title: Who cancels, and how angrily? Measuring the moral content of 8.6 million tweets
text:
Why this mattered
“Cancel culture” gets invoked in newsrooms, legislatures, and product-policy meetings with total confidence and very little measurement. The public debate has three claims baked in: that it is a left-wing practice, that it is about accountability, and that it is one thing. Each of those is testable if you treat the discourse as data. The question for anyone who moderates content, measures brand sentiment, or studies online behavior is the same one: can you measure moral condemnation at scale without fooling yourself, and what does the measurement show?

title: Who cancels, and how angrily? Measuring the moral content of 8.6 million tweets
text:
Data






NoteWhat the analysis used, and what this page can show





The analyzed corpus is 8,572,185 original English-language tweets from 4,035,488 users, collected through the Twitter Academic Research API between November 2022 and January 2023, deduplicated, with retweets removed so the unit is authored text. Platform terms prohibit redistributing tweet or bio text, and the private individuals in Study 5 are reported only in aggregate. Everything on this page is computed from user-level or study-level aggregates; the small CSVs behind each figure are in the site repository. Analysis code is at github.com/zjschroeder/Cancel-Culture-Text-Analysis.

studyName = new Map(labels.map(d => [d.study, d.short_label]))
corpus = [
  {study: "Cancel Culture", tweets: 3907450, users: 1690113, lens: "the #cancelculture meme"},
  {study: "Is Over Party", tweets: 1953936, users: 1069485, lens: "the \"___ is over party\" hashtag"},
  {study: "Academics", tweets: 773339, users: 325957, lens: "65 canceled faculty"},
  {study: "Celebrities", tweets: 1819005, users: 878659, lens: "12 canceled celebrities"},
  {study: "Civilians", tweets: 118455, users: 71274, lens: "7 viral racism cases"}
]

title: Who cancels, and how angrily? Measuring the moral content of 8.6 million tweets
text:
What I did
The pipeline crosses three environments. Python handled ingestion and cleaning (JSON flattening, a deliberately ordered cleaner that keeps emoji and hashtags because affect is the signal, lemmatization with a parallel stemmed branch for a sensitivity check). R and quanteda built sparse document-feature matrices and TF-IDF for tweets and bios separately, then the semantic networks. Heavy jobs, including GPU inference for the transformer classifiers, ran on the University of Oregon’s Talapas cluster through SLURM; the run guide I wrote for it became the lab’s reference.
Three measurement decisions did most of the work.
Partisan lean without asking anyone. Following Essig and DellaPosta (2024), explicit partisan terms in bios were collapsed to a liberal pole and a conservative pole, and every other bio term was scored by its cosine similarity to each pole in TF-IDF space. That gives a categorical lean for the 1 to 8% of users who state a partisan term and a continuous affiliation score for roughly half of all users. The continuous score was validated against the categorical lean and against an independent latent scaling of the same bios (r = .28 to .43 across samples).
Moral content by triangulation, not by one lexicon. Each tweet was scored with the Moral Foundations Dictionary and its crowd-sourced extension, plus MoralBERT (vice/virtue) and Mformer (foundation presence), plus TweetNLP’s RoBERTa emotion, offensive-language, hate, irony, and sentiment classifiers. The outrage measure is the point where the dictionary vice composite and the transformer vice composite agree (r = .28); a one-factor model over the three moral instruments loads positively in every sample. The anger classifier, notably, does not track moral condemnation on this corpus at all, and the page says so rather than hiding it.
Effect sizes on users, not tweets. With samples in the millions every contrast is “significant,” and tweets nest within prolific authors. All contrasts are Cohen’s d on one-row-per-author aggregates, with cluster-robust standard errors and intraclass correlations reported alongside (the design effect runs about 1.2, and the naive standard errors were 2 to 2.3 times too small).

title: Who cancels, and how angrily? Measuring the moral content of 8.6 million tweets
text:
What I found

1. Partisanship is legible in how people describe themselves, even when they never mention politics
Users who share nonpolitical bio vocabulary also tend to share partisan lean. Modularity of the liberal/conservative partition on the bio-similarity network is about 0.13 in the two largest samples, close to Essig and DellaPosta’s benchmark of 0.17, and climbs to 0.20 to 0.35 in the smaller, more sorted samples. Lemmatized and stemmed tokenizations agree, so the pattern is a property of the language rather than the preprocessing.

modularity = [
  {study: "Cancel Culture", users: 265068, lemmatized: 0.127, stemmed: 0.128},
  {study: "Is Over Party", users: 164939, lemmatized: 0.131, stemmed: 0.116},
  {study: "Academics", users: 26105, lemmatized: 0.346, stemmed: 0.275},
  {study: "Celebrities", users: 18485, lemmatized: 0.271, stemmed: 0.210},
  {study: "Civilians", users: 5300, lemmatized: 0.204, stemmed: 0.205}
]
modLong = modularity.flatMap(d => [
  {study: d.study, users: d.users, tokenization: "lemmatized", Q: d.lemmatized},
  {study: d.study, users: d.users, tokenization: "stemmed", Q: d.stemmed}
])
Plot.plot({
  marginLeft: 110, height: 300, width: 720,
  x: {label: "Modularity (Newman-Girvan Q) →", domain: [0, 0.4], grid: true},
  y: {label: null, domain: modularity.map(d => d.study)},
  color: {legend: true, domain: ["lemmatized", "stemmed"], range: ["#2A6B5C", "#C49A45"]},
  marks: [
    Plot.ruleX([0.17], {stroke: "#6b7280", strokeDasharray: "4,4"}),
    Plot.text([{x: 0.17, y: "Cancel Culture"}], {x: "x", y: "y", text: ["Essig & DellaPosta benchmark, Q = 0.17"], dy: -22, dx: 6, textAnchor: "start", fill: "#6b7280", fontSize: 11}),
    Plot.dot(modLong, {x: "Q", y: "study", fill: "tokenization", r: 6, tip: true, title: d => `${d.study} (${d.tokenization})\nQ = ${d.Q}\n${d.users.toLocaleString()} users in network`})
  ]
})























Partisan homophily in bio language: modularity of the liberal/conservative partition, by sample and tokenization. Dashed line is the Essig and DellaPosta (2024) benchmark.




Pooled bio-term semantic network. Node color is cosine proximity to the liberal (blue) and conservative (red) poles; the terms that sit near a pole are mostly not political words.




2. Conservative-leaning users run hotter on outrage and the binding foundations, but the differences are small
Moral Foundations Theory predicts that conservatives lean on loyalty, authority, and sanctity and that the “vice” poles (harm, betrayal, subversion, degradation) should show up more in punitive talk. That is the direction the data take. The size is another matter: the largest contrast is the outrage proxy at d = 0.06. I read this as directional consistency, not a substantial difference, and it still cuts against the folk “left-wing outrage” story.

Does it depend on how big the account is? Splitting by follower tier within the two large samples, the conservative-minus-liberal gap in outrage is present in every tier and largest among everyday accounts, not among the accounts with the biggest audiences.

  ]

Mean outrage proxy by partisan lean and follower tier. Hover for group sizes.



3. Cancellation talk is punitive everywhere, and most punitive toward the least powerful
Splitting morally loaded tweets into a punishment logic (degrade the target) and an accountability logic (center the wronged), punishment predominates in every sample, from 54% to 63% of morally loaded tweets. The tilt is steepest for the meme and the civilian cases and shallowest for academics, which fits a power-relative reading in which the least powerful targets attract the most degrading language. The frame rule was checked against a hand-coded stratified sample.

frames = FileAttachment("data/frames_by_lean.csv").csv({typed: true})
frameData = frames.filter(d => d.lean !== "None" && d.lean !== "Neutral").map(d => ({...d, sample: studyName.get(d.study) ?? d.study}))
Plot.plot({
  height: 340, width: 720, marginLeft: 60, marginTop: 40, marginBottom: 20,
  fx: {label: null, axis: "top", domain: ["Cancel Culture","Is Over Party","Academics","Celebrities","Civilians"]},
  x: {label: null, axis: null, domain: ["Liberal","Conservative"]},
  y: {label: "↑ Punishment share of morally loaded tweets", domain: [0.4, 0.75], grid: true, tickFormat: ".0%"},
  color: {legend: true, domain: ["Liberal","Conservative"], range: ["#2b6cb0","#c0392b"]},
  marks: [
    Plot.ruleY([0.5], {stroke: "#9ca3af", strokeDasharray: "3,3"}),
    Plot.barY(frameData, {fx: "sample", x: "lean", y: "punishment_share", fill: "lean", tip: true, title: d => `${d.sample}, ${d.lean}\npunishment share = ${(d.punishment_share*100).toFixed(1)}%\nn = ${d.n_moral.toLocaleString()} morally loaded tweets`})
  ]
})























Share of morally loaded tweets classified under the punishment frame, by sample and author lean. Bar width is not scaled to n; hover for counts.



4. The right bundles cancel culture with a wider enemy
Phelan (2025) argues that the political right folds woke, CRT, SJW, and cancellation into one interchangeable target. If so, conservative cancellation talk should reach for that cluster vocabulary more often. It does, in every sample with enough authors to trust: in the meme sample the rate is 11.0% for conservative-leaning authors against 7.9% for liberal-leaning ones, about 39% higher. This is the finding I hold with the most confidence, because it is the most direct test of a specific prior claim.



Percentage of a lean group’s cancel-culture tweets containing an ideological-cluster term, by sample.




5. Outrage arrives after the story, not with it
Anchoring each canceled academic, celebrity, and civilian to their own peak-volume day and tracing the outrage rate across a 60-day window, the moral temperature at the peak is near baseline. Outrage accumulates over the following days and crests a week or two later. The initial burst is informational; the condemnation builds behind it. Mean outrage is higher in the month after than the month before for all three target types, and it rises for 67% of celebrities, 60% of civilians, and 50% of academics.

]

title: Who cancels, and how angrily? Measuring the moral content of 8.6 million tweets
section: What a team would do with this
text:
What a team would do with this
A trust-and-safety or brand-listening team would take three things from this project before any of the substantive findings. First, a partisan or ideological signal can be recovered from self-description without asking users anything, and it should be validated against an independent measure before it is used, because the coverage jump (from 1 to 8% to about half of users) comes with a real drop in precision. Second, an outrage or toxicity measure built on one lexicon or one classifier will disagree with the next one; the defensible move is to triangulate and to report the agreement, including the instrument that misbehaves (here, the anger classifier). Third, with millions of records the reporting unit matters more than the test: aggregate to the author, report effect sizes, and cluster the standard errors, or every dashboard number will look decisive.
On the substance, the timing result is the operational one. If moral condemnation crests a week or two after a story peaks, the window for de-escalation, moderation staffing, or a brand response is after the volume spike, not during it.

title: Who cancels, and how angrily? Measuring the moral content of 8.6 million tweets
section: Limits, and what I would do differently
text:
Limits, and what I would do differently
The samples are keyword-filtered, so they over-represent engaged accounts and are not Twitter as a whole. The partisan effects are directionally consistent but tiny, and I would not let anyone quote them without the d. The frame classifier is rule-based and validated on a sample, not on the corpus. Out-of-sample replication (holding out authors, not tweets), cascade and diffusion tests, and a spline model of the dose-response curve are still to come. If I started again I would fix the reporting unit and the triangulation design before collecting anything, since retrofitting both cost more time than the models did.

title: How belonging changes the way students read ambiguous feedback
text:
In brief. Academic feedback is often ambiguous (“interesting approach”), and what a student does with it depends on how they read it. Across an exploratory study (n = 423), a preregistered direct replication with a power analysis and a preregistered effect-size range for success (n = 233), and a preregistered extension (n = 469), lower social belonging predicted more negative evaluation of the same feedback, and the replication landed inside its preregistered range. Published in Social Psychology of Education (2025).

N = 1,125exploratory → confirmatorypower analysispreregistered replication rangeQualtrics

title: How belonging changes the way students read ambiguous feedback
text:
Why this mattered
Feedback is the cheapest intervention in education and one of the least understood. If two students read the same sentence differently because of how much they feel they belong, then feedback quality is not a property of the sentence alone, and improving it means attending to the reader.

title: How belonging changes the way students read ambiguous feedback
text:
What I did
Study 1 was exploratory and generated the hypotheses. Study 2 was a direct replication with preregistered confirmatory hypotheses, a power analysis based on Study 1, exclusion rules fixed in advance, and a preregistered criterion for what would count as a successful replication (an R² range). Study 3 was a preregistered conceptual replication and extension that moved the outcome from forced choice to Likert-type scales. All three ran on Qualtrics with a university participant pool.

title: How belonging changes the way students read ambiguous feedback
text:
What I found
Lower belonging predicted more negative evaluation of ambiguous feedback in all three studies. The Study 2 model landed inside the preregistered replication range. Gender differences appeared in feedback-format preferences.

title: How belonging changes the way students read ambiguous feedback
section: What a team would do with this
text:
What a team would do with this
This is the study I point to when someone asks how I decide that evidence is sufficient. The answer is written down before the data arrive: the hypothesis, the sample size, the exclusions, and the range of effects that will count. That discipline transfers directly to A/B testing and to any program where the temptation is to read a result after the fact.

title: How belonging changes the way students read ambiguous feedback

title: From a CV to a resume: what I cut, and why it hurt
text: The academic CV I defended with ran to four pages. The resume I now send runs to one, and almost nothing on it is phrased the way the CV phrased it. This post is the record of that conversion, written mostly so I remember the rules next time.

title: From a CV to a resume: what I cut, and why it hurt
section: The CV describes what I studied. The resume describes what I built.
text:
The CV describes what I studied. The resume describes what I built.
The first bullet on my old CV said I “synthesized 20 years of video-recorded interviews into a novel dataset examining the linguistic predictors of empathy in interpersonal conversation.” Every word is true and none of it tells a hiring manager what I can do for them. The replacement says what happened, in order: six legacy studies consolidated, 74 hours transcribed with a speech model, a team of research assistants trained to correct it, a segmentation model fine-tuned on 5,000 hand-coded utterances at 96.8% holdout agreement. The topic (empathy) is gone. The mechanics are what transfer.
The general rule I landed on, after reading more career-office guidance than I would like to admit: a resume bullet is a verb, a thing, a scale or tool, and a result. If it does not end with a number or a consequence, it is a responsibility, and nobody hires for responsibilities.

title: From a CV to a resume: what I cut, and why it hurt
section: Titles are for the reader, not the registrar
text:
Titles are for the reader, not the registrar
“PhD Student, Graduate Research Fellow” is what the university called me. It is also nearly meaningless to someone who has never been inside a psychology department. The resume now says “Research Scientist and Statistics Instructor (Graduate Research Fellow),” with the official title in parentheses where a background check can find it. Same job, described for the person reading.

title: From a CV to a resume: what I cut, and why it hurt
text:
Publications became one line
Two peer-reviewed articles and eight conference presentations occupied a page of the CV. They are one line on the resume, with a Google Scholar link. Industry readers do not weigh a publication list; they weigh whether the work was used. So the feedback experiment became a bullet about preregistered replication standards, and the papers moved to the bottom.

title: From a CV to a resume: what I cut, and why it hurt
text:
Numbers must agree everywhere
The most useful thing I did was keep a single master file with every number and its source. The analytic sample for the suspension study is 6,351, not the 17,000 records I had access to. The tweet corpus was 7.8 million collected and 5.5 million analyzed in 2023, and 8.6 million analyzed in the 2026 rebuild; the resume and this site had better say the same thing. A recruiter who spots one drifting number stops believing the rest.

title: From a CV to a resume: what I cut, and why it hurt
text:
What hurt
Cutting the teaching. Thirteen terms of instruction compressed to one bullet, and the courses I was proudest of are not named. Cutting the theatre degree to half a line. Cutting the dog from the summary (he is back on the About page). None of it was wrong to cut; the page is for the reader.

title: From a CV to a resume: what I cut, and why it hurt
text:
The rules, in one place
Rebuild from the job, do not trim the CV. One master file, every number sourced. Verb, thing, scale, result. Titles the reader understands. Publications as a count and a link. Tools named only where they were actually used. One page for analyst roles, two for research-scientist roles, never a page and a quarter. And a plain-text paste test before sending, because a two-column template looks fine and parses as soup.

title: Who cancels, and how angrily? Measuring the moral content of 8.6 million tweets
text:
So what?
“Cancel culture” gets invoked in newsrooms, legislatures, and product-policy meetings with total confidence and very little measurement. The public debate has three claims baked in: that it is a left-wing practice, that it is about accountability, and that it is one thing. Each of those is testable if you treat the discourse as data. The question for anyone who moderates content, measures brand sentiment, or studies online behavior is the same one: can you measure moral condemnation at scale without fooling yourself, and what does the measurement show?

title: Dashboards
text:
I built these to be used either in teaching or for fun as exercises in creating shiny dashboards. All of them run in the browser or on a free host; source is on GitHub.


Teach Yourself SQL
A browser-only Shiny app that teaches SQL to people who already know the basics of R that I built to teach myself SQL. Each tab builds one clause of a query on a live SQLite database then gives users a live editor to test their knowledge. Source


Self-guided Tour of T-Tests and ANOVA
A ground-up visual explanation of common statistical procedures that uses interactive figures to (hopefully) demystify some of the more obtuse concepts. Source


Global Data on Teacher Pay and Job Satisfaction
An interactive dashboard on teacher salaries and working hours (R, flexdashboard, plotly). Source


LA28 Olympic Schedule Builder
In preparation for the LA28 Olympic Games, this little app creates custom schedules for different events based on user interest, budget, and location. First load may take a few seconds while the free host wakes up. Source
